solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Transport two horses, astride black animal

parts.note: a bus is a form of public transport
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

indicators.note: the second horse sits with legs either side of the black letter, so it goes around it

parts.note: a bay is a reddish-brown horse
B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black

explanation.surface: Someone loads two horses into a trailer, one straddling a black animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two horses' supplies two separate horses: H (heroin slang) and BAY; only BAY sits astride B. A bushbaby is a small African primate.
explanation.definitionFit: A bushbaby, or galago, is a small nocturnal African primate, so it is an example of an animal.

clue.text: Bishop was the head of church's local office

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
to run something is to head it, so ran
CH is the standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A bishop once ran his church's local branch.
explanation.definitionFit: A branch is a local outlet of a larger organisation, such as a bank's office in a town.

clue.text: Bones with curves round area towards the top

indicators.note: in a down entry, the letters run upwards, so are reversed
the curves go around the area letter

parts.note: arcs are curves

explanation.surface: Curved bones near the upper part of the body.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacra is the plural of sacrum, the triangular bone at the base of the spine.

clue.text: Spooner's greeting character created by Homer from memory

indicators.note: Spooner swaps the opening sounds of the two words

parts.note: hi is a greeting, said aloud like a word starting with an H sound and ending in a long I
Bart is the son of Homer in The Simpsons; said aloud the vowel sounds as in a word for the chest organ

explanation.surface: A greeting to a character from the ancient poet Homer, recalled by rote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Homer' suggests the Greek poet; it is Homer Simpson, father of Bart. Swapping sounds in HI BART gives 'by heart'.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowing something by heart means having memorised it so it can be recited without looking.

clue.text: Phone one lightly carries about with hostility

parts.note: to bell is British slang for to phone
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the word for lightly holds the word for about within it

parts.note: gently means lightly
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A caller rings someone softly, though hostility is in the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bell' is British slang for phoning someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Belligerently means aggressively and combatively, behaving in an openly hostile way.

clue.text: Like fare the Spanish offer English to return

indicators.note: the whole string is to come back, reading from right to left

parts.note: el is the Spanish word for the
a bid is an offer at an auction

explanation.surface: A Spanish restaurant offers English food that customers send back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like fare' means resembling food: fit to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Fare here means food, and anything edible is fit to be eaten, just as food is.

clue.text: Wife wasting time on some current art provocateur

indicators.note: the wife word loses the time letter, which is used up

parts.note: 'my old Dutch' is Cockney slang for one's wife
an amp is a measure of electric current

explanation.surface: A wife squanders time on a shocking contemporary art provocateur.
explanation.walkthrough: DUTCH for wife comes from Cockney 'duchess'. Marcel Duchamp exhibited a urinal as art.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcel Duchamp was the Dada artist whose readymades, such as Fountain, deliberately challenged notions of art.

clue.text: Number of deliveries bowled with it, rather poorly

parts.note: B is the cricket abbreviation for bowled

indicators.note: these letters are in a bad way, so jumbled

explanation.surface: A cricket bowler's deliveries go rather badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deliveries' suggests balls in cricket, as 'bowled' backs up; here they are births.
explanation.definitionFit: The birth rate counts births per thousand people, and a birth is a delivery of a baby.

clue.text: Group shifting blame seen to lack answer

indicators.note: the letters move about into a new order
one letter must be missing from the shuffled letters

explanation.surface: A group passes the blame around, seen to have no answer.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove A from the letters of BLAME SEEN and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensemble is a group of performers or items considered together as a whole.

clue.text: Everyone scoffing salmon I caught — it's lush

indicators.note: to scoff is to eat greedily, so the word for everyone takes the salmon inside it

parts.note: all means everyone
coho is a species of Pacific salmon
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A diner boasts that everyone wolfed down the salmon they caught, calling it lush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lush' looks like British slang praise for the food; here it is the noun meaning a heavy drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: A lush is slang for a habitual drunkard, someone dependent on drink.

clue.text: Disruptive chat woke flock's dominant member

indicators.note: disrupted letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: the possessive ending is surface only; the bird group's letters are used

explanation.surface: Noisy chatter wakes the flock, led by its top bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The cock of the walk is the domineering leader of a group, like the top rooster in a farmyard.

clue.text: Perhaps knaves is about right for these

definitions.text: Perhaps knaves is about right for these

indicators.note: the rogues surround the letter for right, enclosing it

parts.note: knaves are rogues, or cads

explanation.surface: Someone muses that the word knaves suits a particular set of things.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: knaves (jacks) are playing cards, and the wordplay puts R inside CADS, another word for knaves.
explanation.definitionFit: The knave is a court card in a pack, so knaves are an example of playing cards.

clue.text: Bread to crack when lunch may be taken

parts.note: skin that chaps cracks, so chap means crack
lunch is often at one o'clock, written AT I with the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: Someone breaks bread at lunchtime.
explanation.walkthrough: AT I is 'at one', a typical lunch hour, with I as the Roman one.
explanation.definitionFit: A chapati is a flat unleavened Indian bread cooked on a griddle.

clue.text: Show appreciation of thespian in capital part

parts.note: to clap is to applaud
a ham is an overacting actor

explanation.surface: An audience in the capital applauds an actor's part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part' looks like a role in a play; it is a district of the capital. Clapham is an area of south London.
explanation.definitionFit: Clapham is a district of south London, so it is one portion of the British capital.

clue.text: Nobleman's relative holding page's shiny coat

indicators.note: the relative's phrase keeps the page letter within it

parts.note: an earl's mother is a mother of earl

explanation.surface: An aristocrat's relative wears a page's glossy coat.
explanation.walkthrough: MOTHER OF EARL takes P inside the final word, giving PEARL.
explanation.definitionFit: Mother-of-pearl is the iridescent nacre lining some shells, a lustrous layer or coating.

clue.text: Plot a feature grasped by couple

indicators.note: the pair of letters is held inside the couple word

parts.note: to mate is to couple
the chin is a facial feature

explanation.surface: A storyline element held by a pair of characters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' looks like a noun; it is the verb to scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: To machinate is to scheme or plan intrigues, typically for an evil purpose.

clue.text: Someone in America's fair feature

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an important person, in American slang
second meaning: a Ferris wheel at a funfair

explanation.walkthrough: A 'someone' is an important person; 'big wheel' for that is US usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A big wheel is both an influential figure in American slang and the large rotating ride at a funfair.

clue.text: Where e.g. Arabs may be penning story is not in doubt

indicators.note: the stable phrase encloses the story, as a pen confines animals

parts.note: Arabs are a breed of horse, so they may be in stable
a conte is a short story, from French

explanation.surface: Somewhere horses are kept, someone writes an undisputed story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arabs' are horses here, not people, so IN STABLE is where they may be.
explanation.definitionFit: Something incontestable cannot be disputed, so its truth is certain.

clue.text: Overturned hot vessel with most of that fuel?

indicators.note: in this down entry the pair is turned upside down, reading back

parts.note: a pan is a cooking vessel

indicators.note: the final letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A tipped-over hot pan raises the question of what fuel was used.
explanation.definitionFit: Naphtha is a flammable liquid hydrocarbon mixture distilled from petroleum, used as a fuel and solvent.

clue.text: Pair of horny males in coarse material

parts.note: the first of a pair of horned males: a buck is a male deer, with antlers
the second of the pair, also horned: a male sheep is a ram

explanation.surface: Two lusty males in rough clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'horny' suggests lust, but means having horns: a buck and a ram.
explanation.definitionFit: Buckram is a stiff, coarse cloth of cotton or linen used in bookbinding and to stiffen clothes.

clue.text: Salt dosage in need of amendment

indicators.note: the letters must be corrected into a new order

explanation.surface: A salt dose that needs adjusting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt' looks like the seasoning; it is an old sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: An old salt and a sea dog are both informal names for an experienced sailor.

clue.text: Cat, cat or dog, or dog

parts.note: the cat o' nine tails is a whip
a cat or dog is a typical pet

explanation.surface: A playful list of animals that ends up circling back to a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Cat' is the flogging cat o' nine tails, not a feline.
explanation.definitionFit: A whippet is a slender, fast breed of dog related to the greyhound.

clue.text: One breaking out with key — a whizz!

parts.note: Esc is the escape key on a keyboard
whizz is British slang for urinating, as is pee

explanation.surface: A prisoner breaks out with a key, celebrating as a brilliant operator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'whizz' looks like praise for an expert; it is slang for a pee.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapee is a person who has escaped, such as a prisoner who has broken free.

clue.text: 8th-century pope's a pioneer in quantum science

parts.note: Paul is a papal name used by six popes
the pope of that name who reigned in the 700s was the first, the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A medieval pope is credited as an early quantum physicist.
explanation.walkthrough: Wolfgang Pauli formulated the exclusion principle.
explanation.definitionFit: Wolfgang Pauli was an Austrian physicist whose exclusion principle helped found quantum mechanics.

clue.text: Impeccable performance no longer?

parts.note: ex means former, no longer so
an act is a performance

explanation.surface: A faultless show that has since been retired.
explanation.definitionFit: Exact means precise and correct in every detail, so faultless.

clue.text: Mostly long drinks in all seasons

indicators.note: most of the word is kept, its final letter dropped

parts.note: to long for is to yearn
a round is a set of drinks bought for a group

explanation.surface: Someone mostly longs for drinks whatever the season.
explanation.definitionFit: Year-round means happening throughout the whole year, through spring, summer, autumn and winter.

clue.text: Place in which there's little flipping wiggle room

indicators.note: the place word holds the other inside it

parts.note: to lay is to place

indicators.note: the word for little is turned over, read backwards

parts.note: wee is Scottish for little

explanation.surface: Someone complains of having hardly any blasted room to wriggle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' looks like a mild British curse; it reverses WEE to EEW.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeway is the freedom or margin to act, a degree of latitude.

clue.text: Corner-cutting politician admitted to going downhill

indicators.note: the politician is let into the skiing word

parts.note: skiing is sliding down a slope
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician cutting corners on a downhill run, admitted to a ski resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going downhill' suggests decline; it is literally skiing.
explanation.definitionFit: Skimping means economising stingily, doing the minimum to save effort or money.
